mcqs.question: Which of the following statements correctly defines average velocity?

options.A: Average velocity is the total distance traveled divided by the total time taken.
options.B: Average velocity is the total displacement divided by the total time taken.
options.C: Average velocity is the magnitude of the displacement divided by the total time taken.
options.D: Average velocity is the total distance traveled divided by the magnitude of the displacement.

mcqs.answer: Average velocity is the total displacement divided by the total time taken.
mcqs.explanation: Average velocity is a vector quantity defined as the total displacement (the straight‑line change in position, which has direction) divided by the total time taken. It differs from average speed, which uses total distance (a scalar) in the numerator. Option B states the correct definition; the other options describe speed or mix distance and displacement incorrectly.

mcqs.question: How can the instantaneous speed of a moving object be obtained mathematically?

options.A: By dividing the total distance traveled by the total time of travel.
options.B: By taking the limit of the average speed as the time interval approaches zero.
options.C: By measuring the magnitude of its velocity vector at any chosen instant.
options.D: By averaging its speed over a long period of motion.

mcqs.answer: By taking the limit of the average speed as the time interval approaches zero.
mcqs.explanation: Instantaneous speed is defined as the magnitude of instantaneous velocity, which is obtained as the limit of average speed (or average velocity) when the time interval Δt becomes infinitesimally small: v = lim_{Δt→0} Δs/Δt. Option B captures this limit process. Option C describes the result after the limit has been taken, but the question asks for the mathematical procedure. Options A and D refer to average quantities over finite intervals, not instantaneous values.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly compares instantaneous velocity with average velocity for a particle moving along a straight line?

options.A: Instantaneous velocity is always larger in magnitude than average velocity.
options.B: Instantaneous velocity is the derivative of displacement with respect to time, while average velocity is the total displacement divided by total time.
options.C: Average velocity is a vector quantity, whereas instantaneous velocity is a scalar quantity.
options.D: Instantaneous velocity and average velocity are identical if the motion is non‑uniform.

mcqs.answer: Instantaneous velocity is the derivative of displacement with respect to time, while average velocity is the total displacement divided by total time.
mcqs.explanation: Instantaneous velocity is defined as v = ds/dt, the derivative of displacement with respect to time, giving the velocity at a specific instant. Average velocity over an interval is Δs/Δt, the total displacement divided by the total time. Option B states this exact distinction. Option A is false; magnitudes can be larger or smaller. Option C reverses the nature of the quantities (both are vectors). Option D is incorrect because only uniform (constant) motion makes the two equal.

mcqs.learning_point: Distinguish scalar speed from vector velocity
mcqs.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes scalar speed from vector velocity?

options.A: Speed has both magnitude and direction, whereas velocity has only magnitude.
options.B: Speed is a scalar quantity representing how fast an object moves, while velocity is a vector quantity that includes both speed and direction.
options.C: Speed can be negative, but velocity cannot.
options.D: Velocity is measured in meters per second, while speed is measured in meters.

mcqs.answer: Speed is a scalar quantity representing how fast an object moves, while velocity is a vector quantity that includes both speed and direction.
mcqs.explanation: Speed is the magnitude of the rate of motion and has no direction; it is a scalar. Velocity combines that magnitude with a specific direction, making it a vector. Option B accurately captures this distinction. Option A incorrectly swaps the definitions. Option C is false because speed is never negative, and velocity can have negative components depending on the chosen coordinate system. Option D misstates the units; both are measured in meters per second.
